fd-blaptica-dubia.title: Dubia Roach
fd-blaptica-dubia.summary: A clean, quiet, slow-moving South American roach that has become a favorite staple feeder. Dubias can't climb smooth plastic or glass, don't smell when kept properly, and have a soft shell and good protein.
rows: Live roach; adult males have full wings, females only tiny wing stubs
Adults about 1.5–2 in (sold in several sizes)
About 20–25% protein and 7–9% fat; poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (about 1:3), so dust with calcium
Excellent staple insect when gut-loaded; vary the diet, since very heavy dubia feeding without variety may contribute to gout

Warm is best: about 85°F (29°C) speeds growth and breeding. A smooth-sided tub (they cannot climb smooth plastic), egg crate for hiding, slightly damp (not wet) coco bedding, and a water gel or crystals for moisture

Roach diet plus fresh vegetables and fruit; remove moldy food. Feed them greens, vegetables or a commercial gut-load diet for 24–48 hours before offering them, and dust with calcium (with or without D3, depending on your lighting)
Mature at about 4–6 months; females give birth to 20–40 live nymphs about once a month over a 1–2 year life
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-blaberus-discoidalis.title: Discoid Roach
fd-blaberus-discoidalis.summary: A tan, fairly large roach (sometimes called the false death's head roach) from the Caribbean and northern South America. Like dubias, adults have wings but aren't active fliers and can't climb smooth vertical surfaces, which makes them easy to keep.
rows: Live roach; tan adults with a dark patch behind the head; brown, speckled nymphs
Adults about 1.4–1.8 in (35–45 mm); sold in several sizes
Roach staple in a varied insect diet
Smooth-sided tub with egg crate; they cannot normally climb clean, smooth plastic or glass. Keep most of the tub at about 75–84°F (24–29°C) with a cooler 70–75°F retreat; cooler colonies breed slowly
Feed them greens, vegetables or a commercial gut-load diet for 24–48 hours before offering them, and dust with calcium (with or without D3, depending on your lighting)
Nymphs reach adulthood in about 4–5 months
Caribbean islands, Panama, Colombia, Venezuela, Trinidad and Florida
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-tenebrio-molitor.title: Mealworm
fd-tenebrio-molitor.summary: The classic, inexpensive feeder: the larva of the darkling beetle. Mealworms are easy to keep in the fridge and great for tempting appetites, but they're fatty with a tough shell and poor calcium, so they're best as an occasional food.
rows: Live beetle larvae (giant mealworms are the same species, grown larger with a juvenile hormone that keeps them in the larval stage)
About 18–20% protein and 12–13% fat; very poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (about 1:13)
Occasional treat; the tough shell can cause impaction in young reptiles

Store in the refrigerator at about 38–50°F (3–10°C) in grain bedding (cups can go straight in). Let them warm up 30 minutes before refrigerating; every 5–7 days take them out and give a fresh slice of potato or apple for moisture, and never let it mold
Feed them greens, vegetables or a commercial gut-load diet for 24–48 hours before offering them, and dust with calcium (with or without D3, depending on your lighting)
Keep up to about two weeks in the fridge with little care, or several weeks with the regular feeding routine
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-zophobas-atratus.title: Superworm
fd-zophobas-atratus.summary: A big, wriggly darkling-beetle larva from Central and South America. Superworms are very enticing and softer than mealworms, but they're high in fat and low in calcium, so treat them as a treat rather than a daily food.
rows: Live beetle larvae with dark ends; about 2–2.4 in (50–60 mm) when full size
About 18–20% protein and 14–15% fat; very poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (about 1:13)
Treat or rotation feeder, not a staple
Do not refrigerate: they are tropical and need about 70–80°F (21–27°C). Keep in a plastic tub between layers of grain bedding with a slice of vegetable for moisture; cups keep about two weeks
Feed them greens, vegetables or a commercial gut-load diet for 24–48 hours before offering them, and dust with calcium (with or without D3, depending on your lighting)
Crowding delays pupation; a mature larva goes stiff in a C shape to pupate and emerges as a beetle 1–3 weeks later
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.
warn: Never refrigerate superworms; below about 60°F or above 85°F they quickly die.

fd-manduca-sexta.title: Hornworm
fd-manduca-sexta.summary: The bright green caterpillar of the tobacco hawk moth. Hornworms are juicy and hydrating, low in fat and very attractive to reptiles, but they're low in protein and grow fast, so they're best as a supplemental feeder.
rows: Live caterpillars sold in a cup with their own food
Grow as long as they have food; well-fed worms can reach about 4 in
About 9% protein and 3–4% fat (very high in moisture); calcium-to-phosphorus about 1:3
Treat or supplemental feeder, great for hydration

Keep the cup at room temperature or a little warmer (low 80s °F for fastest growth, mid-50s °F to slow growth). They only eat the formulated hornworm diet and die within about a day of running out, so feed them off before the food runs out. Never let them sit in direct sun or above about 85°F
When a worm stops eating and wanders, it is ready to pupate in soil or paper towels; the moth (wingspan up to about 5 in) emerges weeks to months later
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-galleria-mellonella.title: Wax Worm
fd-galleria-mellonella.summary: The soft, pale larva of the greater wax moth, a beehive pest. Wax worms are irresistible to most reptiles, which makes them handy for coaxing a picky or recovering animal to eat, but they're extremely fatty.
rows: About 14–16% protein and 18–22% fat; very poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (about 1:19)
Rare treat or appetite starter for picky eaters

Store cool at about 50–60°F (10–16°C); the refrigerator door butter tray is often the right spot. Most fridges are colder than that; room temperature with low humidity is better than a fridge below 40°F. Keeps a couple of weeks
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-drosophila-melanogaster.title: Fruit Fly Culture (melanogaster)
fd-drosophila-melanogaster.summary: A ready-made culture of the small fruit fly, the go-to first food for tiny dart frogs, baby geckos and other very small insect-eaters. The culture keeps producing new flies for several weeks.
rows: Live culture: flies, larvae and food medium in a vented cup
Very small (the smaller of the two common feeder fruit flies)
Staple for very small insect-eaters; dust before feeding
Keep at room temperature (about 65–80°F). Cooler slows production; too warm encourages mold and bacteria in the medium. Keep some flies in the culture to keep it producing
About 12–15 days from egg to adult at room temperature; one culture produces several generations over roughly 5–6 weeks
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.

fd-gryllodes-sigillatus.title: Tropical Banded Cricket
fd-gryllodes-sigillatus.summary: A slightly smaller, banded relative of the house cricket. Banded crickets are active and lively, tend to live longer than house crickets and have less chitin, making them easier to digest. Like all crickets, they need gut-loading and dusting.
rows: Live crickets; light tan with two thick black bands
Adults about 0.5–0.7 in (13–18 mm); sold from 1/8 in to 3/4 in
About 18–21% protein and 6–7% fat; very poor calcium-to-phosphorus ratio (about 1:9), so always dust with calcium
Staple feeder when gut-loaded and dusted; movement triggers hunting

Move them out of the shipping box right away into a dry, well-ventilated bin with egg crates. About 70–75°F is ideal (avoid above 80°F or below 65°F). Fresh food and a water gel, replaced every two days; remove dead crickets
Feed them greens, vegetables or a commercial gut-load diet for 24–48 hours before offering them, and dust with calcium (with or without D3, depending on your lighting)
Probably native to southwestern Asia; now widespread in the tropics worldwide
notes: Never feed an insect larger than the space between your pet's eyes.
warn: Don't leave uneaten crickets in the enclosure; they can bite reptiles.
